 After building a film career that gained widespread recognition later in life, Morgan Freeman continues to pursue acting as he approaches 90. In an August 2026 interview with The New York Times, the actor discussed his motivation to keep working, his role in Taylor Sheridan's Lioness and his perspective on aging.
 Freeman's career gained momentum when he was 50, following years of preparation and work in theater. His recent projects include reprising his role as U.S. Secretary of State Edwin Mullis in Lioness in 2026 and releasing a blues album, according to the source report.

 Freeman shared his perspective on maintaining a positive outlook as people grow older, emphasizing the importance of appreciating everyday abilities and continuing forward.

 "If you can get out of bed and don't fall down when you do it, then you just count your blessings and keep moving."
 The statement came from Freeman's August interview with The New York Times, in which he discussed his character's White House storyline and the considerations involved in accepting new acting roles. He said receiving a script written with him in mind remains exciting, although he now evaluates compensation and potential script changes before committing to a project.
 Freeman also drew on a philosophy associated with Clint Eastwood, whose advice was to keep aging from becoming a reason to stop pursuing one's interests.
 Also Read 
 Lively and Reynolds Face Questions Over Baldoni TV Appearance 
 "Don't let the old man in."
 Freeman said he intends to continue working while opportunities remain available. His approach reflects a willingness to stay active rather than treating age as a reason to leave the industry.
 "I'll work as long as I can — as long as somebody says, 'Do you want to do this part?'"
 Also Read 
 Ellen DeGeneres Settles in the Cotswolds After Leaving Hollywood 
 Freeman began pursuing acting after serving in the U.S. Air Force as a mechanic and realizing that flying was not his ultimate ambition. During the 1950s, he moved to Los Angeles to study performing arts at City College before making progress on Broadway. His breakthrough in film came with Street Smart in 1987, earning him his first Academy Award nomination.
 His subsequent roles included Nelson Mandela in Clint Eastwood's Invictus and God in Bruce Almighty. Freeman also won an Academy Award for his performance in Million Dollar Baby, further establishing his place in Hollywood .
 Although Freeman acknowledged that his enthusiasm for acting has decreased somewhat over time, he continues to welcome new challenges. When asked by The New York Times whether any particular roles remained on his wish list, he indicated that he no longer had specific ambitions to fulfill.
 Also Read 
 John Travolta Honors Kelly Preston on Her Birthday 
 "No. I'm pushing 90 now. So, the roles that I wished I had been able to play, Denzel Washington will play."
 Freeman has also discussed perseverance and maintaining perspective in previous interviews. In a 2012 interview with The Talks, he described the importance of seeking enjoyment and peace despite life's difficulties.
 "I'm making a great effort because sometimes life is not enjoyable. Sometimes it's painful and sometimes it's stressful, sometimes it's agonizing even, so I think once you get around those humps: Strive for pleasure and peace."
 Also Read 
 Billy Crystal Describes Faith Loss After Home and Friend Deaths 
 In a 2016 interview with Esquire, Freeman explained how focusing on a clear objective can help people pursue what they want.
 "One of the things I say to young people, particularly my kids, is: 'You get what you want.' I'm making [a] distinction between 'want' and 'would like to have.' What you want is what you're going to put on the refrigerator door.
 You're going to focus on that and get it. It's going to happen. It's unstoppable."
 Also Read 
 Jennifer Lawrence Addresses Chris Pratt Affair Rumors From Passengers 
 Freeman offered a related perspective on professional responsibility in a 2025 interview with The Guardian, emphasizing the importance of doing good work rather than concentrating on outcomes beyond one's control.
 "I don't know if I actually can say I've learned a lesson. What I try to do is good work; do your job and the rest will take care of itself."
